pinterest.title: Mexican Wedding Traditions: Padrinos, the Lazo, the Arras, Mariachi and the Tornaboda
pinterest.description: Mexican wedding traditions belong to the whole family. Padrinos and madrinas, the wedding sponsors, each carry a role in the Mass, from the lazo and the arras to the kneeling cushions and the bouquet. The civil ceremony makes it legal, then come the mariachi, the money dance, la víbora de la mar and the tornaboda the next day. Our guide walks through each custom in the order the day unfolds, for Australian couples marrying in Mexico or at home.

pinterest.title: El Lazo: How Padrinos Place the Wedding Lasso at a Mexican Wedding
pinterest.description: The typical Mexican wedding lazo is two rosaries joined to form one. It is placed at the nuptial blessing, after the Our Father, when the padrinos de lazo lay it over the couple, and it is lifted away at the end of the ceremony. In some communities these sponsors must be a stable couple married in the church, as an example to their godchildren. Choose them with care, and brief your photographer: the moment comes quickly.

pinterest.title: La Víbora de la Mar: The Sea Snake Dance at a Mexican Wedding Reception
pinterest.description: La víbora de la mar has become a popular wedding dance in Mexico. The couple stand on chairs facing each other and join hands to make an arch, and guests link up in a long line and run beneath it, faster as the music speeds up. With the couple, the víbora stands for the problems they will face: whatever the obstacles, they stay together and do not let go. Have two steady guests beside each chair.

slides: Mexican wedding traditions you did not know, in the order the day unfolds
A Mexican wedding belongs to the whole family. Parents, grandparents and godparents play a part long before the ceremony.
It often begins with la pedida de mano, the asking for the bride's hand. In many communities it takes several family visits, and the decision is shared.
Padrinos and madrinas, the wedding sponsors, each carry a role in the Mass: the rings, the arras, the lazo, the kneeling cushions, the bible and the bouquet.
The lazo, two rosaries joined as one, is laid over the couple at the nuptial blessing. The groom then places the arras coins in the bride's hands.
In Mexico the civil ceremony is the legal marriage. A church wedding does not replace it, so couples who want a Mass plan both.
Then the party: mariachi, the money dance, la víbora de la mar and, the next day, the tornaboda with close family and friends.

instagram_carousel.caption:
A Mexican wedding belongs to the whole family, and the sponsors carry the objects that make the Mass their own.

The padrinos de lazo lay the cord over the couple. The groom places the arras coins in the bride's hands. The madrina de cojines sets the kneeling cushions, and the madrina de ramo looks after the bouquet. Then the mariachi plays, guests line up for the money dance and run beneath the couple's joined hands in la víbora de la mar.

There is no single script. Customs vary from family to family and state to state, so the best first step is a simple one: ask both families early which customs matter most to them.

Our guide walks through each custom in the order the day unfolds: la pedida de mano and the serenata, the padrinos and madrinas, the lazo and the arras, the Mass and the civil ceremony, the music, the dances, the wedding cookies and the tornaboda. It closes with what Australian couples need to know about marrying in Mexico, or bringing these customs home.
